summary:
Casiopea is a browser game where players design, launch and fly a complete space mission across the solar system. Players choose a destination and science objective, then configure the spacecraft, instruments, launch vehicle, orbit and trajectory while balancing mass, power, budget, fuel, data, communications, risk and mission lifetime. Every decision has consequences: a better instrument adds science value, but also mass, power, cost and data. The mission is then flown in 3D: liftoff from Cape Canaveral, orbit departure, a cruise through asteroids, orbit insertion, landing and a rover secondary mission. A final evaluation explains why the mission succeeded or failed.

We used NASA data wherever possible, with sources cited in the game: planetary parameters from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet (NSSDCA), past-mission counts from the NASA NSSDCA Chronology of Lunar and Planetary Exploration, landmark missions such as Mariner 2, Apollo 11, Viking 1 and Voyager 2, and NASA Blue Marble imagery of Earth. The game follows the process in NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions, Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab resources.

Casiopea turns abstract engineering trade-offs into hands-on experience, so students learn by trying, failing and redesigning, just like real mission teams.
details:
Casiopea is an interactive, browser-based game that takes players through the whole life of a space mission, from the first idea to the final science report. It is available at https://casiopea-spaceapps.vercel.app and needs no installation or account.

  1. Choose a destination. The game opens with an animated Big Bang that forms the solar system. Players then pick a destination: Mercury, Venus, the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Neptune. Each one shows its real gravity, distance, temperature, atmosphere and how many missions have explored it before.
    • a difficulty level: Basic, Intermediate or Advanced;
    • a mission type: Orbiter, Flyby, Lander, Rover, Atmospheric probe, Crewed or Sample return;
    • a science objective, such as mapping the surface, searching for water and ice, or studying rock and soil composition.
    • liftoff from a Kennedy Space Center–style launch complex at Cape Canaveral, with thrust control;
    • an orbit-departure burn inside a timing zone, and spacecraft stabilization;
    • a cruise dodging asteroids, space debris, micrometeoroids and solar storms;
    • orbit insertion or atmospheric entry;
    • a powered landing on a real landing site such as Gale Crater, Jezero Crater or the Shackleton crater rim.
  2. Run the science. After landing, the player drives a rover across procedurally generated terrain to reach the science targets. Along the way they climb slopes, avoid hazards such as dust devils, dust storms and solar flares, and manage battery and time limits.
  3. Learn from the result. The evaluation explains why the mission succeeded or failed. Players can retry with the same design, or reconfigure it and fly again.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission design is usually taught as separate topics: orbits in one class, spacecraft subsystems in another, budgets somewhere else. Casiopea brings them together in one experience, so players see how changing one subsystem affects the whole mission. Students and newcomers can experiment, fail safely and redesign, the same way real mission teams learn through trade studies.

The game explains concepts in plain language and is fully bilingual (English/Spanish), so it works for players with different levels of knowledge. Our goal is to make space engineering more accessible to students in Latin America and beyond, and to spark interest in STEM careers.

NASA data and resources

We used NASA data wherever possible, and the sources are cited inside the game:

  • NASA Planetary Fact Sheet (NSSDCA): gravity, distance, temperature and atmosphere for every destination.
  • NASA NSSDCA Chronology of Lunar and Planetary Exploration: the number of previous flybys, orbiters, landers and rovers at each destination. This history affects gameplay: less-explored worlds carry more risk and narrower margins.
  • Real NASA missions: Mariner 2, Apollo 11, Pioneer 10, Viking 1, Voyager 2, Cassini–Huygens and MESSENGER appear in the game’s “History of Space Missions” timeline, so players can compare their design with real ones.
  • NASA Blue Marble imagery: used for the 3D Earth during launch, with Cape Canaveral in its real position.
  • NASA mission-design resources: the game follows the process described in NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions, JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels and the Mission Design Lab. That covers the launch, space, ground and user segments, as well as trade studies, point design and a pre-launch review.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript.
  • Graphics: three.js (WebGL) for the 3D scenes; the Canvas 2D API for the HUD, the Big Bang animation and the mission timeline.
  • Hosting: Preact as a lightweight runtime for the public version, deployed on Vercel.
  • Demo video: Python, Playwright and FFmpeg.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop. The game runs in any modern browser.

What makes it creative

  • Design decisions are tested in playable mini-games instead of a static configurator. The thrust you set, the burn you time and the asteroids you dodge all depend on the spacecraft you built.
  • Real history shapes the gameplay: destinations explored by many missions are easier, and rarely visited worlds are riskier.
  • The intro turns the formation of the solar system into a cinematic Big Bang, and landmark NASA launches fly across the map.
  • The secondary rover mission puts the player in the role of a planetary scientist, not only an engineer.

Scalability and future development

Casiopea was built to grow. The game engine is data-driven: planets, landing sites, spacecraft components, instruments, launch vehicles, orbits and trajectories are all defined in data tables. Adding a new destination, mission type or launch vehicle means adding an entry, not rewriting the game. Each screen is an independent module. The whole game is a static web app served from a global CDN, so it can serve many players at almost no cost and has no servers to maintain.

Planned next steps:

  • Team mode for up to four players, with roles for mission planning, spacecraft design, science and communications, negotiating trade-offs together.
  • New worlds: moons such as Europa, Titan and Enceladus, plus asteroids and comets, with new mini-games such as a rotorcraft flight on Titan and a touch-and-go sample collection on an asteroid.
  • Live NASA data: real planetary positions and launch windows from JPL Horizons, and trajectories validated with NASA’s GMAT.
  • Save, share and compare: export mission designs, global leaderboards and competitive scenarios where teams solve the same objective.
  • Classroom tools: a teacher dashboard, guided lessons aligned with STEM curricula, and mission reports that students can submit.
  • More reach: more languages, full mobile and tablet support, and a VR mode to explore missions in 3D.

What our team considered

  • Accessibility: plain-language explanations, three difficulty levels, on-screen and keyboard controls, and bilingual text.
  • Realism vs. fun: real data and real trade-offs, simplified enough to stay playable.
  • Meaningful feedback: the game explains why a mission failed, not just a score.
  • Replayability: multiple destinations, mission types, objectives and random events.
  • Availability: a free public link that works on any computer, with no installation or registration.
